articles.title: Unprotected license plate surveillance cameras let anyone with a web browser tune in
articles.summary: The Verge is about technology and how it makes us feel. Founded in 2011, we offer our audience everything from breaking news to reviews to award-winning features and investigations, on our site, in video, and in podcasts.
articles.body: Automated license plate recognition systems, also known as ALPR or simply LPR systems, have become increasingly popular — and controversial — tools for law enforcement in recent years. The systems can automatically photograph and record data on license plates in real time, drawing the ire of privacy advocates like those at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which has just released information on security vulnerabilities in ALPR systems across the country. “Earlier this year, EFF learned that more than a hundred ALPR cameras were exposed online, often with totally open Web pages accessible by anyone with a browser,” the organization says in the new report released today. The report focuses on systems sold by a company called PIPS Technology, which is now owned by 3M. According to the EFF, live feeds from some of the cameras were available to watch online, and “were individually connected to the internet and freely accessible online to anyone who knew where to look.” The organization described its testing approach: The testing process involved confirming that a camera was online and responding to requests by connecting to it with a Web browser or by connecting to it over Telnet. If the camera had a password on both the Web and Telnet interface we left it alone, but if the camera was not protected with a password we were able to recover configuration information. However, when the Web was locked down, but Telnet was not, we [were] able to view password information in the Telnet configuration. Often these passwords were set to the default or were otherwise not sophisticated enough to be secure.Using information embedded on the page and through publicly available sources, the EFF was able to identify the position of some of the cameras, and got in touch with the owners to highlight the vulnerabilities. Some, like local Louisiana law enforcement agencies and the University of Southern California, took steps to fix the vulnerabilities. But the city of Hialeah, Florida, stopped returning the organization’s calls. The ACLU has found that about three-quarters of law enforcement agencies were using similar systems in 2011, giving officers “hundreds of millions of data points” on drivers not accused of a crime.

articles.title: Dozens of Flock AI camera feeds were just out there
articles.summary: The livestreams connected to dozens of Flock’s AI-powered surveillance cameras were left available on the internet for anyone to watch, according to findings from YouTuber Benn Jordan and 404 Media.
articles.body: The livestreams connected to more than 60 of Flock’s AI-powered surveillance cameras were left available to view on the web, allowing someone to see live feeds of each location without needing a username or password, according to findings from tech YouTuber Benn Jordan and 404 Media. Flock is a technology company that works with thousands of law enforcement agencies and businesses to deploy a network of AI-powered cameras across the country. It also recently partnered with Ring, giving Flock customers the ability to request footage from users in Ring’s Neighbors app. As noted by 404 Media, many of Flock’s cameras are made to scan a vehicle’s license plates. However, the feeds exposed to the internet connect to Flock’s Condor cameras, which can pan, tilt, and zoom to automatically track people and vehicles. “I watched a man leave his house in the morning in New York,” Jordan says in his video. “I watched a woman jogging alone on a forest trail in Georgia. This trail had multiple cameras, and I could watch a man rollerblade and then take a break to watch rollerblading videos on his phone. How? Because the camera’s AI automatically zoomed in on it — just like it zoomed in on a couple arguing at a street market in Atlanta.” [Media: Jordan worked with Jon “GainSec” Gaines — who previously uncovered security flaws within Flock’s system — to find the live feeds on Shodan, a search engine containing a database of devices connected to the internet. As reported by 404 Media, the two located dozens of Flock live feeds and administrator control panels, where they could not only view the streams but also freely download video archives from the last 30 days, change settings, delete footage, view log files, and run diagnostics, as reported by 404 Media and Jordan. Anyone with links to the stream could access them, no credentials required, according to 404 Media. In some cases, Jordan and 404 Media’s Jason Koebler visited the locations of the Flock cameras, where they were filmed and displayed on the openly accessible livestreams. “This was a limited misconfiguration on a very small number of devices, and it has since been remedied,” a Flock spokesperson said in a statement to 404 Media. Flock didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

articles.title: Betting operators and prediction markets spent record amounts on campaign donations and lobbying
articles.summary: Sports-betting and casino companies want to win back millions of bettors and gambling dollars that prediction markets have lured away.
articles.body:
Casino operators and sports betting companies have spent record amounts on campaign donations and on lobbying in Washington thus far this year, hoping it will help win back millions of bettors and gambling dollars that prediction markets have lured away.

Sportsbook operators, including FanDuel and DraftKings, have funneled more than $80 million into state senate and congressional races, via Win for America, a PAC launched in November 2025. The casino industry's primary lobbying group, the American Gaming Association, has spent a record $2.06 million through September — the biggest lobbying spend by the group since 2013, when online gambling was reinstated after being banned in 2006.

Prediction markets and some of their executives have also been spending on local elections and on lobbying — primarily spending on the campaigns of politicians who oversee and shape their regulatory body, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Kalshi executives, including co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, have contributed more than $1.6 million directly to campaigns and to PACs supporting both political parties — nearly as much as the $1.79 million, including $1.28 million to outside firms, the company has spent on lobbying thus far this year. Polymarket has spent $270,000 via outside lobbying firms this year, and has made a $1 million donation to a Democratic nonprofit, according to a private remittance document seen by Reuters. And a new PAC, Coalition for Prediction Markets, backed by Kalshi, along with prediction market operators Robinhood, Coinbase, Crypto.com, and Underdog have spent an additional $200,000.

"Kalshi's political giving reflects our strong relationships with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle," John Bivona, Kalshi's head of federal government relations, said in a statement, adding that their giving reflects the company's belief that keeping prediction markets safe "isn't a partisan issue."

Lobbying efforts are to "support the responsible development of federally regulated markets," a Coalition for Prediction Markets spokesperson said. Polymarket declined to comment, and FanDuel, DraftKings, and Win for America didn't respond to requests for comment.

Prediction market companies are fighting against several state attorneys general, who argue that the sites operate as illegal online gambling operations and should be shut down, limited to non-sports betting or regulated on a state-by-state basis instead of by the federal agency.

Sports betting companies are hoping to retain their footholds in more than 30 states amid new scrutiny of the industry. Some recent studies have highlighted addiction problems, and some organizations have raised alarm bells that the rise in youth gambling is a public health crisis, which has motivated policymakers to propose legislation to regulate sports betting.

articles.title: Social Security kept paying a dead Florida woman for nearly 6 years — and her great-niece cashed in. Who's on the hook?
articles.summary: The law is pretty clear: Social Security fraud comes with severe consequences.
articles.body:
A Florida woman who passed away kept receiving her Social Security retirement benefits for nearly six years — and her great-niece was cashing in.

Asha Anderson, 48, of Pompano Beach, Florida had been withdrawing her great-aunt's benefits from ATMs between April 2017 and December 2022 — to the tune of more than $152,000, according to prosecutors.

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Now Anderson has been found guilty of both Social Security fraud and theft of government funds, meaning she could face fines and jail time.

If the Social Security Administration (SSA) keeps paying benefits after someone dies, who's on the hook? The law is pretty clear about this one.

Social Security fraud comes in many forms. For example, fraudsters might target you by pretending to work for the SSA so they can obtain your personally identifiable information, such as your Social Security number. Then, they can use that information to commit identity theft and file claims under the stolen SSN.

But fraud also relates to submitting false information on a claim, misusing someone's benefits who's incapacitated or collecting someone's benefits after they pass away — either hiding their death or simply not bothering to report it.

**"**Under federal law, collecting funds from a deceased beneficiary constitutes federal Social Security fraud and theft of government property," writes Dmitry Gorin, a partner with Eisner Gorin LLP, in a blog post. "This serious federal crime carries penalties including felony charges , federal prison sentences, mandatory financial restitution and substantial fines."

It's possible you spent the funds without any fraudulent intent. After all, the death of a loved one comes with an enormous amount of administrative work at a time when you're experiencing an enormous amount of grief.

In cases where there's no criminal intent to commit fraud, you'll still have to repay any posthumous payments.

But intentional deception or willful concealment is a different matter altogether. In those instances, you'll have to repay the stolen funds, but you could also face substantive jail time.

articles.title: Rick Lazio: We’ve lost an auto race before, China’s EV climb should worry us
articles.summary: New tech won't help if U.S. factories can't produce it efficiently. Automakers and suppliers need incentives to invest in robotics and advanced equipment.
articles.body:
Tesla's newly unveiled Roadster is a reminder that America can still produce breakthroughs that capture the world's imagination. The car can accelerate from zero-60 in less than a second and perform feats that once belonged in science fiction.

The engineering is thrilling. Give Tesla an A for design innovation. The harder question is whether it can commercialize even the base Performance model. It includes the fan-powered suction system but none of the thrusters behind the Roadster's headline-grabbing acceleration or airborne maneuvers. Or will Chinese manufacturers use their state-supported supply chains and generous R&D incentives to make comparable technology affordable first?

Chinese automakers are already gaining ground in Britain with vehicles that combine advanced technology and aggressive pricing. The Jaecoo 7, a Chinese-built SUV nicknamed the "Temu Range Rover," became Britain's best-selling new vehicle in September . Chinese brands captured nearly a quarter of the country's new-car market that month.

American ingenuity is not the problem. The challenge is converting it into affordable products at scale, something China has become remarkably effective at doing. The next auto race will be decided by which country can excel at both.

Americans have been largely shielded from direct competition with Chinese automakers. The United States imposed a 100% Section 301 tariff on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024, effectively closing the market to them. The policy sought to prevent the heavily subsidized vehicles from undercutting domestic production.

The rationale is understandable. American companies operating in a market economy cannot compete on equal terms with a state-directed industrial system. China spent years supporting battery production and vehicle manufacturing, giving its automakers advantages that tariffs are meant to counter.

The problem is, protection alone cannot make an American factory more productive, lower the cost of a battery, or bring a better vehicle to market.

American automakers have learned this lesson once already.

During the 1970s and 1980s, Japanese competitors won over American consumers with better fuel economy and higher quality. They also found more efficient ways to build cars. But American companies were slow to respond. One recent analysis estimates that the Big Three took between 10 and 15 years to catch up with Japanese advances in production efficiency .

Policymakers recognized that American companies needed a stronger reason to invest in innovation. Congress responded in 1981 by creating the federal research and development tax credit amid concern about declining private-sector R&D spending and U.S. competitiveness. The same principle applies today. New discoveries matter only if companies have the incentive and capital to bring them to market.

articles.title: IRS issues fresh warning to US taxpayers: ‘Sensitive’ data now at risk. Act before mid-November to protect your refund
articles.summary: Taking the right steps can make all the difference.
articles.body:

For Americans counting on a tax refund to pay down debt, rebuild savings or catch up on bills, having someone else file a fraudulent return in their name could turn a financial lifeline into a paperwork nightmare.

The IRS is urging taxpayers to take steps now to protect their personal information — including one some taxpayers should take before an essential mid-November deadline.

In an Oct. 22 release (1), the agency advised Americans to safeguard their IRS online account credentials and obtain an Identity Protection PIN to help prevent criminals from misusing their identities.

"Protecting sensitive financial information is essential to preventing unauthorized users from accessing confidential tax information and IRS online services," said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano.

He added that those precautions can help taxpayers "protect themselves from bad actors."

Tax-related identity theft occurs when a criminal uses your Social Security number to submit a false return claiming a fraudulent refund. According to the IRS, your tax account is particularly vulnerable (2) when stolen information includes both your Social Security number and financial details, such as wages.

And resolving a suspicious return can stand between you and your money.

The IRS says (3) its Taxpayer Protection Program may send a letter asking you to verify your identity and return information. Until you respond, the agency cannot process the return or issue the refund.

The IRS offers a free tool to help protect you: an Identity Protection PIN, or IP PIN.

This six-digit number helps the agency confirm your identity and prevent someone else from filing a federal return using your Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number.

You can request one from the IRS (4) even if you aren't required to file a return. For taxpayers planning to file early in 2027, the IRS recommends acting before its online PIN system becomes unavailable for annual maintenance in mid-November. It generally becomes available again in mid-January.

articles.title: Government contractor arrested for allegedly leaking national defense information
articles.summary: Federal authorities arrested a government contractor and charged him with leaking classified national defense information, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced on Friday. FBI investigators have accused 42-year-old Ian Brinksman, an employee of a third-party company which provided services to a government agency, of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, who writes an online…
articles.body:
Federal authorities arrested a government contractor and charged him with leaking classified national defense information, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced on Friday.

FBI investigators have accused 42-year-old Ian Brinksman, an employee of a third-party company which provided services to a government agency, of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, who writes an online publication on Substack.

“A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 claimed Individual 1 had “published reporting based on classified [relevant U.S. government agency] assessments.” Individual 1 posted on her social media profile, “I also accept leaks,” the DOJ said in its release.

Brinkman was arrested following a search of his Washington, D.C., home.

Quotes included in the affidavit match the description of posts to the Capital & Empire Substack, a Congress and defense publication written by Aida Chavez.

Chavez did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment. Chavez’s past work has appeared in The Hill, according to her bio on the social platform X.

In the DOJ’s statement announcing Brinkman’s arrest, FBI Director Kash Patel said any employee caught leaking classified information will “be met with the full weight of justice.”

“Protecting America’s secrets is a top counterintelligence priority of this FBI – and anyone caught abusing their position of trust within the government by jeopardizing national security and putting our brave warriors at risk will be met with the full weight of justice,” Patel said.

Identifying and prosecuting leakers has been a priority for the second Trump administration, threatening prosecution of both the government employees and media organizations that publish leaks.

In July, the DOJ moved to subpoena four journalists from The New York Times for their reporting on a luxury jet gifted to the president by Qatar, which was used as Air Force One but has periodically been pulled for security concerns .

Trump is not the first president to vow to go after leakers or to subpoena journalists — former presidents Obama, George W. Bush and Nixon did the same.

articles.title: Security forces deploy as Milan braces for another day of protests
articles.summary: The Italian government has sent hundreds of soldiers to the country’s financial hub ahead of anticipated unrest.
articles.body:
Milan, Italy – Protests have been called in eight Italian cities on Saturday to demonstrate against Giorgia Meloni’s right-wing government and the rising cost of living, a week after demonstrations in Milan spiralled into clashes with police and looting.

It follows the announcement online of a new round of protests by a newly formed group calling itself the ‘October 17 Movement’, which has been the main driver of demonstrations alongside student federations, grassroots trade unions, and antiwar coalitions.

“Those who deny our future are truly violent,” it said on Instagram. “We distrust this government because we see it as authoritarian.”

In response to last weekend’s looting, the government announced a series of new security measures, including the deployment of 500 soldiers to Italy’s financial hub.

On Friday, police carried out raids and searches in several cities, against people suspected of taking part in looting and rioting in last weekend’s protests, the Italian news agency Adnkronos reported. Officers conducted another 150 raids on Saturday morning in the northern region of Lombardy.

But on its Telegram channel, the October 17 Movement said many of those planning to demonstrate wanted to voice their dissent peacefully.

“We must be peaceful. If we give [the police] an excuse, they will charge against us,” a participant identified as E said on Thursday.

Others have stressed that there is no distinction between those who engage in violence and peaceful protesters. “It’s just us,” said a member identified as Q.

Protesters decided to keep the location of the demonstration secret until the last minute. Three meeting points were expected to be announced on their social media accounts on Saturday afternoon.

In the meantime, police confirmed to Al Jazeera that they had located and were questioning the administrator of the group’s Instagram page. According to the Italian daily Corriere della Sera, he is a 30-year-old Italian-Moroccan freelance journalist and researcher. He is currently under investigation on suspicion of “inciting crimes”.

Most of the protesters arrested on Sunday were very young. Of the 271 people arrested, 220 were under the age of 18.

Some joined the protests after being unexpectedly added to a Telegram group, Corriere della Sera reported.

“They said that they would raise chaos and we could take a lot of goods,” one of them said.

Lawyer Michele D’Agostino is defending two demonstrators, aged 21 and 15.

“[The youngest one] didn’t even know the reasons behind the protest; he had just seen it on TikTok and decided to check it out with a friend,” D’Agostino told Al Jazeera.

“He was not among the looters, but he did not realise the seriousness of what was happening,” he said.

The public prosecutor has blamed social media for misleading young people into taking part in what he described as “insurrectional acts”.

Meanwhile, Justice Minister Carlo Nordio told Sky TG24 that there was a need to “expand the capacity of our youth detention facilities” in response to the mass arrests of people under the age of 18.

Earlier this week, truck drivers set up roadblocks in several regions of southern Italy to protest soaring fuel prices, leaving many markets without supplies for days. On Thursday, the government sought to offer them some relief by granting tax breaks and establishing a special fund for farmers and fishermen.

articles.title: PHP-ocalypse: How two critical web bugs almost broke the internet | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Two critical bugs in the PHP web programming language, used by the majority of the internet, threatened to upend the internet — and it's unlikely to be the last major software scare.
articles.body:
On Wednesday, a decades-old open-source web technology called PHP almost broke the internet, thanks to two vulnerabilities that had sat dormant for years until researchers recently figured out a way to exploit them.

The bugs are dubbed PHP2Shell , officially designated as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 . In simple terms, the bugs allow anyone who knows how to exploit them to break into an online system running PHP, such as a website or internet-facing server, without needing a password to access or modify its data.

As situations go, this was a pretty sizable one, forcing millions of people around the world to scramble to patch their systems before malicious hackers could abuse them.

The PHP Foundation, which maintains the PHP web software, publicly released patches on Wednesday that fixed the bugs, which when installed prevent web-facing servers from being attacked. The foundation had already given some of the biggest internet companies and web hosts that rely on PHP an early headstart on patching.

Thanks to weeks of backroom chatter and careful coordination across the industry, the world — so far — broadly avoided mass internet exploitation. From Wednesday, governments began urging citizens and companies with websites to take action to mitigate the risks on their ends. A wide range of industries shuttered their websites and pulled services offline to patch their systems. Banks, retailers, gaming sites, online stores, hospitals, and some government agencies took down their servers to prevent attacks.

But security researchers are warning that the situation isn’t over yet, and that a large number of systems around the world remain unpatched and vulnerable to hacks and data theft.

This is also unlikely to be the last major internet software scare, with some expecting the advent of AI to rapidly uncover as-yet-undiscovered vulnerabilities that are waiting to be found and abused.

Security researchers at Calif found two bugs in PHP, a programming language widely used around the world for building websites and web apps, both on the internet and hosted locally on company networks, like intranets and internal sites.

PHP is open-source, meaning it’s free and available to be used by anyone for almost any reason. As such, it’s become one of the most popular and broadly used web programming languages on the web today.

The two bugs were first discovered in 2024 but weren’t considered exploitable at the time, and weren’t patched. Security researchers recently found a way to exploit them, prompting them to alert the makers of the software to get them fixed.

Calif alerted the PHP Foundation, which began a period of fixing the bugs and coordinated disclosure. The foundation did this by offering the information and patches about the security issues under a tightly guarded embargo — essentially held confidentially until a specific deadline — to give big companies an opportunity to get ahead of installing the fixes.

PHP2Shell is pretty serious because it can be abused remotely over the internet and without the victim having to click on a link or open a file. This is known as remote code execution , and it’s one of the more damaging kinds of bugs to exploit because they can grant a hacker anywhere in the world effectively full control over an affected and unpatched system.

Worse, these specific PHP bugs make it possible to break into any unpatched system on the internet without needing a password or any other credential over the internet, known as unauthenticated access.

This would allow a malicious hacker to then plant malware on the computer, such as to steal data or simply to maintain a long-term foothold that they can return to later.

The bugs are particularly risky because PHP is wildly popular software, in part because it’s free and relatively easy to use, but also because it’s been around for decades. Around 70% of the web-facing internet relies on PHP, though its usage has been slowly declining over the years in favor of newer, more secure programming languages.

Given its popularity, some of the world’s most popular websites are run on web software that rely on PHP, such as WordPress (which hosts TechCrunch!), as well as Drupal, Joomla, and MediaWiki, which powers online encyclopedia giant Wikipedia.

PHP is just one of many aging but functional technologies that have survived waves of the internet and generations that are now so ubiquitous, they’re akin to the glue that holds much of the internet together. Oftentimes these tools are developed by open source maintainers, who are not paid for the work that they do, and as such cannot afford third-party security reviews — but are still widely relied on by companies who do not contribute financially to the projects.

Security researchers at Calif were credited with discovering the bugs earlier this year as part of a security audit of PHP’s code. Calif was participating in the Hack the Planet initiative by AI model maker OpenAI and cloud security giant Wiz, which subsequently verified the proof-of-concept exploits that Calif made.

In Calif’s write-up (featuring comics — it’s great, check it out ), the researchers explained that AI was used in assistance with exploiting the bug, but that the bulk of the work relied on knowledge that the researchers already had, and that they knew PHP’s codebase and exploitation history well.

“No model is simply capable of unearthing ‘all bugs’ with simple prompts. At least for now,”wrote Calif.

Despite efforts to keep details of the bugs under wraps until Wednesday, it does appear that there was some PHP2Shell exploitation prior to the release of patches.

Amazon, which has enormous visibility into online threats due to its size and scale, said in a blog post that it detected exploitation of PHP2Shell about a week before the PHP patches were available, suggesting that someone, somewhere, knew how to exploit the bugs before their details were broadly available. Amazon said it wasn’t clear how the hacker learned of the vulnerabilities, but that defenders should look for evidence of exploitation as early as October 17.

There are a few theories as to what happened. Once a bug is patched, the details of the patch can become immediately apparent, especially if the code — like in PHP’s case — is open source, making it public and inspectable. Exploiting the bugs might not be easy, but knowing where the bug is and how it was fixed can allow malicious hackers to understand where to target and how to develop their exploits.

It’s possible that there was a leak or a breakdown in communication somewhere during the embargo. The open source community is enormous and controlling information in this fashion relies on good-faith.

It’s also possible that hackers discovered the bugs ahead of time, either independently or through espionage.

The PHP Foundation blamed one company for pushing the patches live hours before the embargo period was up, which could have given some attackers a headstart if they obtained details of the patch before others. But this doesn’t account for the week-long activity detected by Amazon.

Researchers say that bugs require a lot of work to become exploitable and weaponizing the bug has been a challenge — but not impossible — which explains why we haven’t seen a scale of mass-exploitation just yet.

But as of late Friday, there are now confirmed compromises and post-exploit activity related to the PHP bug, according to security giants Palo Alto Networks and Trail of Bits . That means the bug was detected being abused to hack in and actively do malicious activity on an as-yet-unknown target.

Large parts of the internet shut down, but are returning. Did we dodge the worst of it?

It’s still early days but it’s an encouraging sign that there haven’t been any signs of mass-exploitation — but we’re not out of the danger-zone just yet.

Matthew Prince, the chief executive of network security and monitoring giant Cloudflare, which also has telemetry into a vast portion of the internet, said this week that it’s seen an exponential number of attempts to exploit the bugs following their disclosure. This gives some perspective as to how quickly malicious actors are seeking to abuse the flaws for their own gains.

PHP isn’t just found on web servers, but also used in developer tools, command line and terminal packages, and other software components used by routers, storage devices, and enterprise security devices, like firewalls and VPNs.

We should expect to see exploitation of PHP2Shell down the line as smaller IT teams and sole developers may be slower to update. There will also be a period in which various companies that rely on and integrate PHP into their own products and software, which will also need updating.

As more devices and systems get updated, the attack surface will reduce in time. But the ripple effects of these bugs could still be felt for years to come, particularly in legacy systems that have no means to be updated.

This was one of those rare internet-stopping days I’ve seen during my time as a security reporter. In 2016, a massive botnet flooded internet registry Dyn with junk traffic causing much of the web’s top services to crawl to a halt. In 2017, North Korea used leaked U.S. government hacking tools to infect the U.K.’s health system with ransomware. And in 2024, a faulty CrowdStrike update sparked a massive global outage causing most of the world’s Windows computers to crash at once.

By all accounts with PHP2Shell, the internet escaped what could have otherwise been an extremely painful and damaging day. But it’s unlikely to be the last major incident to hit the web, and this may be the first in a trend of incidents that exploit weaknesses in legacy technology. Much of this is due to inherent flaws in aging but omnipresent software that haven’t yet been discovered, coupled with AI tools that are making it easier to find flaws.

PHP, much like other web programming languages and technologies from decades ago, are “memory unsafe,” which means they can be attacked through an entire class of vulnerabilities that can force the software to leak or spill sensitive data from the software’s memory storage. The National Security Agency says around 75% of all actively exploited vulnerabilities abuse memory-related flaws, which is to say, hackers use them a lot.

This has helped to prompt a move to using memory-safe languages, like Python, Rust, and Swift, which can’t be abused in the same way that memory vulnerabilities can be. As such, these languages make them broadly immune to a broad swath of vulnerabilities that still affect their predecessors.

But that still leaves an entire chunk of the internet running a bunch of technologies, like PHP, media and video codecs, compression libraries, and other software from decades ago — which, when they break, will have massive implications for the rest of the web.

articles.title: How MAHA fueled a new wave of doctors running for office
articles.summary: Dozens of medical professionals are running for Congress and top state offices this midterm season, a direct Democrat-led counteraction to the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda’s outsized influence on national health policy. There are seven physicians running for congressional office in this election, including Democrats Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Amish Shah…
articles.body:
Dozens of medical professionals are running for Congress and top state offices this midterm season, a direct Democrat-led counteraction to the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda’s outsized influence on national health policy.

There are seven physicians running for congressional office in this election, including Democrats Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Amish Shah in Arizona and Richard Pan in California. There are even more nurses — 14 non-incumbent candidates — running for Congress, according to Nurse.org’s Nurses on the Ballot research series.

Among Republican non-incumbents, neurosurgeon John Cowan of Georgia and internist Ralph Alvarado of Kentucky are both running for the House.

With four nurses and 20 physicians in Congress — four in the Senate and 16 in the House — the number of doctors and nurses currently running outnumbers those in office.

On the campaign trail, physician candidates have leaned on their medical backgrounds, including their work responding to recent public health emergencies, when making their case as to why they are suited for federal office.

Physicians consistently rank high among Americans when it comes to trustworthiness. And the Democratic Party seems intent on tapping into this.

A KFF Tracking Poll released in June found that more participants said they trusted their “own doctor or health care provider” than federal authorities like the Food and Drug Administration, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, President Trump or Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

These results echo what the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) of the University of Pennsylvania found in March , when 86 percent of those surveyed said they trusted their primary care provider for trustworthy public health information, compared to 38 percent who said the same about Kennedy.

“People are really looking for public servants,” said Celinda Lake, a Democratic political strategist and president of Lake Research Partners. “They really love their local firefighters, teachers, nurses, doctors. They really trust them, and trust and honesty is the number one trait that people are looking for right now in a political official.”

It’s no coincidence that this wave of medical professionals is moving toward Congress in an era defined by the COVID-19 pandemic, rising healthcare costs and the ascent of MAHA. Campaigns strategists say extreme healthcare conditions and policies have pushed ordinary physicians into becoming politicians.

“What MAHA has been good for is recruiting them, because so many of them see what’s going on and feel like they have to speak up. Because a lot of medical professionals have no desire to enter into politics, and this is a fairly new field for them. And I think what MAHA did was help energize them to run,” Lake said of the new class of physicians running for office.

Andrews, a pediatrician running against Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) to serve a full term in the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s seat, has explicitly said she decided to run after Kennedy was nominated to be Health and Human Services secretary.

Pan, also a pediatrician and former member of the California state senate, has similarly said he is running because he believes Congress needs people with the training to “hold this administration accountable.”

314 Action, a political action committee dedicated to getting Democrats in STEM into office, declared 2026 would be the “year of the doctor” and this year marks the first election since the group launched its Guardians of Public Health recruitment campaign to get more healthcare professionals into office.

Across both congressional and state legislature races, 314 Action is supporting more than 120 medical professionals as candidates.

Former Director of the Ohio Department of Health Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, is among the candidates that 314 Action is backing. Her race was thrust to the center of the national stage this week after her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ran an attack ad featuring her mother, whom Acton last saw at the age of 12 due at least in part to allegations of abuse at the hands of her stepfather.

“We are really excited about her race, and she really draws a stark contrast between a serious candidate who is looking to serve her community in a new way, and whatever you want to call Vivek Ramaswamy,” said 314 Action President Shaughnessy Naughton.

Should either Andrews or El-Sayed win their respective races, they would be the first Democratic M.D. in the Senate since former Sen. Ernest H. Gruening (D-Alaska) left office in 1969.

Andrews would be the first Democrat who also practiced medicine in the Senate since former Sen. Royal S. Copeland’s (D-N.Y.) term ended in 1938. El-Sayed graduated from medical school and served as the executive director of the Detroit Health Department, but he never completed a medical residency or held a medical license, a fact his opponent former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) has used as an attack .

Recent polling has found that both El-Sayed and Andrews’s races are tight, with neither having a strong lead over their GOP opponents.

While several of these candidates like El-Sayed and Pan have held public offices before, others are new to the political scene. According to Naughton, physicians have a unique advantage when it comes to running for office due to what their jobs entail.

“The advantage for a lot of doctors is that they often have a very public-facing job where they have to counsel people in the most intimate of settings and talk them through really complex processes and concerns that they might have to lead them to make decisions that will benefit their health,” said Naughton.

articles.title: NFL forced to close ‘NFL House’ pop-up due to Paris protests
articles.summary: The NFL closed its fan zone in Paris Saturday due to intense street protests, but the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh Steelers are still set to play the league’s first game in France Sunday, despite President Trump suggesting it push the face-off back. Fans received a notification through the NFL’s “OnePass” app that the “NFL…
articles.body:
The NFL closed its fan zone in Paris Saturday due to intense street protests, but the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh Steelers are still set to play the league’s first game in France Sunday, despite President Trump suggesting it push the face-off back.

Fans received a notification through the NFL’s “OnePass” app that the “NFL House” would be closed, citing “accessibility issues,” according to The Associated Press. The Saints similarly announced in a Saturday morning post to social platform X its fan event in Paris had been rescheduled to the following day.

Trump told reporters outside the White House Friday the NFL “probably could have postponed,” saying it looked like Saturday “is going to be a bad day in France.”

“I would’ve said the NFL could’ve probably postponed that match,” the president said. “France is really in trouble. That’s what happens when you go left.”

The president’s statement seemingly contradicted Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Wednesday comments that U.S. officials felt it would be “fine” to hold the game. The State Department has issued a security alert for Americans traveling in the country.

“Violence and rioting have recently occurred in France and may continue. Avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest. Stay away from areas with large crowds or significant police activity,” the department’s alert reads.

Paris, alongside other cities in France, have been rocked by demonstrations from young people, angry with the government over the state of the education system and the cost of living.

The Steelers and Saints still plan to kick off Sunday at 9:30 a.m. EDT in Stade de France. The game, one of nine NFL matches being played abroad this season, is part of an effort by the league to spread football internationally.

articles.title: Your credit can look normal while someone steals your identity
articles.summary: A clean credit report doesn't mean your identity is safe. Six ways criminals can steal from you without triggering a credit monitoring alert.
articles.body: You check your credit score, see nothing unusual and assume your identity is safe. But what if someone has already stolen your personal information and your credit report shows absolutely nothing? That's entirely possible. Credit monitoring can help detect certain types of identity theft, particularly fraud involving new credit accounts. However, criminals can also target your existing bank accounts, retirement savings, government benefits and phone number without triggering a traditional credit alert. As a result, a clean credit report can give you a false sense of security. Here's what credit monitoring can catch, what it might miss and how to better protect yourself. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. IDENTITY THEFT PROTECTION IS CHANGING: WHAT TO LOOK FOR What credit monitoring actually watches Credit monitoring tracks changes to your credit file. Depending on the service, it can alert you to suspicious activity involving your credit history. Common alerts include: These alerts can help you discover new account fraud before the damage grows. However, credit monitoring depends on information that lenders and other companies report to credit bureaus. Therefore, it cannot reliably detect identity theft that occurs entirely outside the credit reporting system. Six ways criminals can target you without triggering credit monitoring Criminals have several ways to misuse your information, steal money or make you more vulnerable to fraud without triggering a traditional credit monitoring alert. Here are six situations worth watching for. 1. Existing bank account takeover A criminal gains access to your existing checking account, savings account, retirement account or payment app. Because the account already exists, the takeover may never appear on your credit report. Instead, you might first discover the theft through an unfamiliar transaction or a notification from your financial institution. 2. Government benefits and tax fraud Someone uses your Social Security number to file a fraudulent tax return or claim government benefits. You may receive an IRS notice about a tax return you never filed. Alternatively, you could discover unemployment benefits claimed in your name. Neither situation necessarily changes your credit score. 3. Medical identity theft A thief uses your health insurance information to receive medical care, prescriptions or equipment. You might then receive bills for services you never used. Even worse, someone else's medical information could end up in your records. Traditional credit monitoring generally will not detect the misuse itself, although unpaid debts could eventually create other financial complications. 4. SIM swap and phone account fraud Criminals may convince your mobile carrier to transfer your phone number to a SIM card or device they control. Once they have your number, they may intercept certain verification codes and attempt to access your accounts. A sudden loss of cellular service could be an early warning sign, especially if you did not request a change. 5. Scams involving direct payments A scammer tricks you into authorizing a wire transfer, sending money through a payment app or purchasing gift cards. Because you initiated the payment, even under false pretenses, traditional credit monitoring may have no indication that anything happened. Your financial institution might have separate fraud detection systems, but those protections vary. 6. Personal information exposed through data brokers Your name, phone number, address and other personal details may appear on people-search websites or data broker databases. Criminals can use that information to create convincing phishing messages or impersonation scams. Although the exposure itself does not necessarily mean someone has stolen your identity, it can make you a more attractive target. The Federal Trade Commission identifies unauthorized bank withdrawals, unfamiliar medical bills and fraudulent tax filings among the warning signs of identity theft. SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW Why checking your credit score isn't enough A credit score provides a snapshot of your creditworthiness based on information in your credit file. It does not show every account you own, or every place someone might use your personal information. For example, someone could access your retirement account while your credit score remains unchanged. Similarly, criminals might use your phone number to get into an existing account without ever applying for credit. That's why it's important to review your actual credit reports rather than relying on your score alone. Even then, you'll need to check your other accounts separately. How to spot identity theft your credit report can't catch Fortunately, you can look for suspicious activity without paying for an expensive monitoring service. Start with these six habits. 1. Review your financial accounts regularly Check your bank statements, investment accounts, retirement accounts and payment apps for unfamiliar transactions. Also, enable transaction and security alerts whenever your financial institutions offer them. 2. Watch for suspicious tax activity Pay attention to IRS notices about returns you did not file or income from employers you don't recognize. You can also review your federal tax account through the official IRS website at irs.gov/ . You can also request a free six-digit Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) from the IRS. This helps prevent someone else from filing a fraudulent federal tax return using your Social Security number. The IRS issues a new IP PIN each year. 3. Check your Social Security earnings record Review your earnings history periodically to see whether it matches your actual employment. You can access your information through your my Social Security account at ssa.gov/myaccount. Unexpected earnings may require further investigation. 4. Review medical bills and insurance statements Look for unfamiliar medical appointments, prescriptions, procedures or insurance claims. If something looks suspicious, contact your health insurance company or medical provider directly. 5. Protect your mobile phone account Ask your carrier about account PINs, port-out protection and SIM swap safeguards. Additionally, consider using an authenticator app or security key instead of text-message verification when available. 6. Check where your personal information appears online Search for your name, phone number and address to identify information exposed through people-search websites. You can request removal from individual sites or consider a reputable data removal service. Pro tip: Choose one day each month to review your accounts and important records. You can combine it with a bill-payment routine to make the habit easier to maintain. How identity theft protection services can help Credit monitoring remains useful, but it cannot catch every type of identity theft. Some identity theft protection services offer broader monitoring that can help identify suspicious activity involving financial accounts, personal information and online accounts. However, the features and level of protection depend on the provider and plan you choose. What to look for in identity theft protection Before signing up, compare the features, coverage limits and costs. Pay attention to which financial accounts qualify for monitoring and whether the service offers restoration assistance if identity theft occurs. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com Remember: No identity theft protection service can prevent every scam or detect every instance of fraud. These services work best alongside strong passwords, multifactor authentication, account alerts and regular reviews of your financial statements. What to do if you discover identity theft If you suspect someone is using your information, act quickly. You do not need to wait for a credit monitoring alert. You can also review your credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com. The FTC confirms that free weekly online reports are available from the three nationwide credit bureaus. Kurt's key takeaways I always encourage people to keep an eye on their credit, but I wouldn't rely on a credit score to tell me whether my identity is safe. Someone could be accessing an existing financial account or misusing personal information without causing any immediate change to that score. That's why I recommend checking financial statements, turning on account alerts and taking advantage of additional safeguards when they're available. Identity theft protection services can provide another layer of monitoring, but you still need to pay attention to activity in your accounts. When was the last time you checked your bank accounts, medical statements or phone account for signs of identity theft rather than relying on your credit score? Let us know in the comments below. articles.title: Volkswagen Plans New Audi Plant in Georgia, Handing Trump a Win
articles.summary: Volkswagen AG will build a new factory for its premium Audi brand in Georgia and expand a facility in South Carolina, Donald Trump will announce Saturday, as...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Volkswagen AG will build a new factory for its premium Audi brand in Georgia and expand a facility in South Carolina, Donald Trump will announce Saturday, as the US president looks to notch a political win in the final stretch of the midterm election cycle.

The German automaker is also hopeful the announcement will yield potential relief from tariffs that have severely eroded profits.

Volkswagen will build a new plant in Macon, Georgia, to manufacture the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 models, with construction of the greenfield project due to begin soon, according to a US official involved in the talks. The facility will have the capacity to produce 200,000 vehicles per year, the official said.

Volkswagen will also expand its Scout Motors plant under construction in Blythewood, South Carolina, adding 25,000 units per year of capacity for a model yet to be determined, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail the plans. Trump is set to tout the Volkswagen announcement Saturday night during a political rally in Perry, Georgia — a short drive from Macon — where he is trying to boost Republican candidates who are either trailing or effectively tied with Democrats in the polls.

In exchange, Trump and the company will remain in talks on some kind of tariff reprieve, though any changes would apply to all manufacturers who expand US production, not just Volkswagen and its brands, the official said. Talks are focused on a potential deal that would give some sort of proportional tariff relief credit to manufacturers that bring concrete commitments of new production to the US, the official said.

It generally takes years to build a new auto assembly plant, meaning production likely won't begin until later this decade. Audi presented the proposal in the last few weeks to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who relayed it to Trump, the official said.

The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment and a spokeswoman for Audi declined to comment.

The new site gives Trump a fresh commitment of investment and jobs in the battleground state, where polls show GOP Senate candidate Mike Collins trailing Democratic incumbent Jon Ossoff — but a governor's race that is essentially a tossup. Trump has been campaigning to drum up support for Republicans to avert broad GOP defeats in the midterm elections next month, with key races in traditionally red states such as Kansas and Texas now considered to be in play for Democrats.

articles.title: Fed Set to Lead G7 Trio in Hawkish Rate Pause: Eco Week Ahead
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve and its peers in the euro zone and Japan will probably keep interest rates steady in the coming week, opting to bide their time before po...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The Federal Reserve and its peers in the euro zone and Japan will probably keep interest rates steady in the coming week, opting to bide their time before potential further hikes.

Three days of decisions starting on Wednesday in Washington are likely to affirm a hawkish stance balanced by a measured pace as policymakers confront inflation risks ranging from surging energy prices to the artificial intelligence boom.

The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023 and signaled another increase was likely this year. While US inflation data has come in hot since then, officials seem in no rush to deliver another hike. Instead, economists and investors expect a move at the final meeting of 2026, in December.

Chairman Kevin Warsh, who's eschewed guidance on future moves, will face a tricky test at his post-meeting press conference. He probably won't offer much insight about December, but may also not want to sway market bets away from the current expectation for a hike.

Fed watchers may need to wait until after the meeting to hear what other US central bankers say about the prospects for policy.

"We still see the Fed on hold through year-end. Higher borrowing costs are working their way through the economy, and there's a risk that an AI-related market correction around the midterm elections could tighten financial conditions abruptly."

Anna Wong. For full analysis, click here

The European Central Bank on Thursday could offer its own signals on a hike in December, in a decision overshadowed by France's bond-market troubles. The following day, the Bank of Japan will probably keep its rate steady while holding the door open to a move at the end of the year.

In contrast to the no-change expectations from those big-three Group of Seven decisions, other central banks may well deliver action.

Most forecasters anticipate a hike from New Zealand on Wednesday, while several economists see the first such move in three years materializing at the Bank of Canada on the same day.

Elsewhere, US and euro-zone growth data, the UK budget, and rate decisions from Colombia to Thailand will be among the highlights.

articles.title: Will AI expose the rickety infrastructure of the internet?
articles.summary: The moment you realize the internet is "held together by glue and dreams."
articles.body:
A startling announcement went out earlier this week: Due to recently discovered vulnerabilities in the open source programming language PHP, website owners had to immediately patch their sites — or if they couldn’t update right away, they should take the sites down to be safe.

On this week’s episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed the significance of the PHP-ocalypse and whether we’ll see more incidents like this in the future.

Sean called this “a real reckoning moment” that highlights how “when you get down to the bone level of the internet,” everything seems to be “held together by glue and dreams.” And with widespread access to large language models and AI agents, it’s only going to become easier to find these vulnerabilities. (That said, these specific vulnerabilities were found by human researchers , not AI models.)

Kirsten, meanwhile, wondered if we’re about to see the “next level of prepper doom […] because you could see how banks could get exploited, and [with] data and privacy concerns, it just feels a lot bigger than we can fix right now.”

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.

Sean O’Kane: The internet is breaking in lots of ways this week, it seems.

I think the best way to think about this, if people are coming into this kind of cold: How many times over the last 10 years have we had these moments where something breaks or something nearly breaks, where one person maintaining one tiny repro repository as a hobby or whatever happens to catch that something nefarious is going on and and saves us from the infrastructure of the internet completely crumbling?

Now multiply that by a billion, when people have access to not only extremely advanced software in the form of these LLMs that everybody uses, but also the ability to task them to go out and do it themselves, with creating AI agents that are single-minded at accomplishing those things.

We’re seeing a balance of two things happening this week. One is a bunch of the labs and companies like Google and OpenAI actually had people go out and find a bunch of vulnerabilities, including the one with PHP. And then we also have a bunch of people seeming to rush to take advantage of those vulnerabilities to try and hack into websites. So we have governments taking down websites, we have really popular websites that are going down briefly to be able to fix this vulnerability.

This is a real reckoning moment, where we’re going to find out the downside risk of building so much of the internet on open source technology like PHP. When you really get down to the bone level of the internet, it is held together with glue and dreams.

Anthony Ha: There’s so many things that were striking about this. One of them is the fact that — as I understand it, at least — this is not a new vulnerability. This is a vulnerability that has existed in PHP for decades.

And PHP has been used as a programming language to build so much of the web, so this vulnerability has been there for decades, but no one knew about it. What happened is, essentially, that these big AI companies — including Wiz, now owned by Google — they were able to find these vulnerabilities using LLMs. [As noted above, I got this wrong: Human researchers participating in OpenAI and Wiz’s Hack the Planet initiative found the vulnerabilities , though they used AI to exploit the bug.]

I guess part of the calculation is, we need to patch this, because if we can find this vulnerability using LLMs, so can other people. But the only way we can get the patch out there is to announce the vulnerability. And so it creates this very panicked situation where [they say]: “Okay, this vulnerability existed for decades. You have to patch right away, and if you can’t patch it right away, just take your website down. It’s that severe a vulnerability.”

Kirsten Korosec: I think that the important thing is, a lot of people don’t even realize that their websites have PHP — which is this, as you mentioned, decades-old open source programming language.

For those who don’t know, Hypertext Preprocessor is the official term, [it’s] this really the core ingredient behind content management systems that are used throughout WordPress, Drupal, something like 70% of websites. We’re talking tens of millions of websites. So to me, it’s the scale. It also made me immediately think two things: One, this is just the beginning. What other decades-old bad software is out there that is going to be exploited?

And the other one was something that 404 Media, which had a really great breakdown , mentioned, which is link rot. Because a lot of people, companies, governments, maybe that small neighborhood website, they’re shutting these [websites] down. And so we’re going to have so much link rot and also websites that maybe had a little piece of history out there that aren’t gonna be accessible anymore, as opposed to patching it.

Sean: Anthony, I think you made a really good point. I’ve seen a lot of people unhappy with the disclosure rollout here, a bit of the chest beating that OpenAI seems to have done in its post about it.

Also, it seems like a couple people got ahead of the embargo of this release, which set off a race among the hacker set. I think it was Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince [who] already posted about seeing it escalate to millions of attempted hacks of the PHP2Shell.

The thing with these vulnerabilities, the way in cybersecurity this typically works is, if you’re you’re stress testing a company’s software, even if it’s a fundamental piece of software that helps run a lot of different computers or parts of the internet or whatever it might be, you can go to that company and and disclose it and it sort of stays within that bubble. But when we’re talking about something that’s as deep as and as fundamental as this, you can’t go around and tell everybody discreetly.

I mean, maybe you could, if the AI was advanced enough and you could task a billion agents to go send an email to every single person who has control over some part of a website. We are now rueing the days when we had webmasters who were easily identifiable, and maybe that would have solved the problem to some extent. But there’s just no easy way to do this. I think this is the beginning of what’s going to be a lot of back and forth and clearly a new frontier in cybersecurity.

Kirsten: Matthew Prince’s social media post was to me really telling, and pretty scary. Also, I don’t know if either of you saw this, but Amazon also put out a blog post . This is a very well-capitalized company, so they have the tools and a team to sort of catch what’s going on. They operate, basically, a honeypot network, or a decoy, and they actually saw that there were attempts to exploit that vulnerability before it had been publicly announced.

To me, again, it goes back to this: Amazon has the tools and the capital and the know-how to fight these things. There’s so many websites and even potentially government websites that just don’t have that level of attention. And so to me, that’s really the scary part.

And there [are] some AI employees out there that are probably going to take this to the next level of like prepper doom, because you could see how banks could get exploited, and [with] data and privacy concerns, it just feels a lot bigger than we can fix right now. So I’m interested to see two things. One, how extreme people’s behavior gets — but also I’m wondering if some new startups are going to pop up as a result of this, or if we’re going to be turning to some of the open source tools [offered by companies like Nvidia] to create these security layers.

articles.title: Pentagon drafts Iran attack plans as Tehran threatens aggressive retaliation
articles.summary: The U.S. military has drawn up options to potentially attack Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, possibly renewing the conflict that has lasted over eight months. The U.S. Central Command (Centcom), which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, has plans ready to conduct follow-up strikes against Iran if there’s authorization from the White House,…
articles.body:
The U.S. military has drawn up options to potentially attack Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, possibly renewing the conflict that has lasted over eight months.

The U.S. Central Command (Centcom), which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, has plans ready to conduct follow-up strikes against Iran if there’s authorization from the White House, a source aware of the plans, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told The Hill.

Centcom has a number of strike options in place, which are presented to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, another source aware of the planning said.

President Trump will leave all of his options open until he has to make the final decision, this source, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, said.

“To me, it looks pretty likely that the U.S. goes back to military strikes on Iran once the midterm elections are passed,” Gregory Brew, an Iran expert at Eurasia Group, said in a Friday interview with The Hill.

Harrison Mann, a former executive officer of the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) Middle East/​Africa Regional Center, said there are two forms of escalation Trump’s could exercise if he chooses to hit Iran: return to attacking Iranian military and political targets inland or targeting civilian and energy infrastructure if the Israeli military is involved.

“I emphasize inland because since April, the U.S. has basically not attacked anything except for targets on Iran’s coasts. It has apparently not flown aircraft except for maybe one or two strikes over Iranian territory,” Mann said in a Friday interview with The Hill. “That was probably both to reduce the risk of escalation and because they were not willing to risk having more planes shot down.”

“The other path; these are not mutually exclusive, and which becomes more likely if Israeli forces are involved would be going directly targeting civilian infrastructure, energy infrastructure, or as we saw the Israelis do at the start of the conflict, universities, police stations, other civilian stuff,” Mann continued.

When asking the Defense Department for a comment, a Pentagon official said the department’s “job is to develop and present military options to the President.”

“We don’t speculate on hypothetical situations or future operations,” the official said.

Centcom did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The appetite for authorizing kinetic actions comes as the U.S. government looks to pull major concessions from the Islamic Republic amid stalled diplomatic negotiations. Trump himself has warned the U.S. could attack Tehran following the November midterms, where Republicans are fighting to retain both chambers of Congress.

The Trump administration sees Iran’s economy getting weaker by the day, with the combination of sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade degrading the country’s economy, where inflation is rising.

“Basically, using force to add to the existing pressures that are on Iran, force them to capitulate, reach a deal, and allow the U.S. to exit the war,” Brew said, adding that part of why the U.S. is considering military strikes is “frustration” with the lack of progress on the diplomatic front.

“The Iranians are not bending; they’re not showing any flexibility,” he said. “They have a negotiating position that they’ve been sticking to now for several weeks.”

On Monday, Hegseth visited U.S. troops in the Middle East along with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.

“We’ve worked with the Israeli military quite a bit. That’s nothing new. We have for a long time. They have great capabilities, and we appreciate their contributions to assuring Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth told reporters on Tuesday in Wisconsin, praising Israel as “good partners.”

Some regional analysts question if another U.S.-Israel strike campaign — which contributed to the depletion of the Pentagon arsenal of missile interceptors and some exquisite offensive systems, spiked gas prices and rocked the Middle East — would force the Iranian leadership to make concessions.

“There’s no level of U.S. or Israeli strikes that is going to compel Iran to change course at this point. Iranian leaders not only saw themselves in a fight for personal survival and survival of their regime,” Mann, a former Army major, said. “They’ve increasingly come to understand that they have leverage, they have the upper hand, and they want to drive that advantage to try and get concessions from Trump.

“I think we have already seen quite clearly what the limits are of U.S. and Israeli strikes,” he continued. “It could not destroy Iran’s military capacity, could not destroy its political leadership, even though it assassinated key members.

During the active stage of the war, the U.S. and Israeli militaries destroyed and damaged Iranian launchers and missile magazines. Last month, the Pentagon said the U.S. military destroyed upwards of 90 percent of Iranian ballistic missiles, naval industrial base and drones.

Trump has previously pulled back from greenlighting kinetic strikes against Iran after the Pentagon would prepare a strike package.

The U.S. military currently has over 50,000 service members in the Middle East and about 20 warships, some of which are helping enforce the naval blockade in the Arabian Sea.

There are two aircraft carrier strike groups in the Middle East and a third one, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, is going to the Centcom region to possibly relieve the USS George Washington.

The Pentagon dispatched 4,000 Marines and sailors aboard three warships, led by USS Makin Island, a Wasp-class amphibious assault ship, to the Middle East as part of the amphibious readiness group.

The additional battleships and personnel could provide the president with greater options for amphibious landings and other operations.

Trump has also telegraphed that the U.S. military could strike Pickaxe Mountain , located near the damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility in the Zagros Mountains. But some experts have argued the facility’s depth could mean that the U.S.’s most powerful bunker-buster bombs are not likely to penetrate it, as the site is buried up to 2,000 feet below granite.

On Wednesday, the State Department ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their family members from Saudi Arabia as the Iran-backed Houthis continue to attack the Kingdom.

U.S. intelligence found that Iranian plots to target and kill U.S. officials in the Middle East have “substantially increased,” with efforts reaching “advanced stages,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel,” Clayton said in a memo to Rubio, who also serves as Trump’s national security adviser. “The lethal plotting efforts by Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.”

Iranian leaders have signaled privately and publicly that the retaliation in the event of U.S. or Israeli attacks is going to be “bigger,” “more aggressive” and “different” than earlier this year, Brew said.

Tehran is threatening to hit U.S. bases, warships, oil pipelines, refineries and U.S. allies in the Gulf, as Iran still has drone and missile capabilities.

The potential for renewed hostilities in the region, which was reported earlier by The New York Times, also comes as oil prices reached their highest point since May.

The potential for renewed hostilities in the region also comes as oil prices reached their highest point since May .

Brent crude oil surpassed $117 a barrel on Friday, while U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate traded around $102.

“In particular, regional officials and leadership members have been explicitly saying that undersea cables in the Persian Gulf, AI data centers and tech-related infrastructure, all of these will be regarded as targets to be fired on in an event that Iran comes under attack,” Brew noted.

Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and Trump’s special envoy for Syria and Iraq, indicated there could be military action against Iran over the weekend.
